title: Choosing & Committing

learn.summary: Most language projects die in month two, not because the language is hard but because the goal was vague. The US Foreign Service Institute (FSI) has timed this for decades: a Category I language like Spanish takes a full-time learner roughly 600-750 class hours to professional proficiency, while Category IV languages like Mandarin or Arabic take about 2200. Pick one language, name a concrete target (e.g. CEFR B1 in 12 months), and write down why it matters to you personally.

do: Write a one-paragraph commitment note: which language, why, and your 12-month CEFR target. Pin it where you study.
Block a fixed 30-minute daily slot in your calendar for the next 30 days.

children.title: FSI Difficulty Categories

learn.summary: FSI sorts languages into four categories by hours-to-proficiency for English speakers: Category I (Spanish, French, Dutch) ~600-750 hours, Category II (German) ~900, Category III (Russian, Hindi, Thai) ~1100, Category IV (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Arabic) ~2200. This is not a reason to avoid hard languages; it is a reason to budget honestly. A Category IV language at 30 minutes a day is a multi-year project, and knowing that upfront prevents quitting in disappointment.

do: Look up your target language's FSI category, then compute your realistic timeline: category hours divided by your weekly study hours.

children.title: CEFR Levels as Goalposts

learn.summary: The Common European Framework of Reference defines six levels: A1-A2 (basic), B1-B2 (independent), C1-C2 (proficient). B1 is the famous tipping point: you can handle travel, describe experiences, and hold imperfect but real conversations. Use levels as milestones, not vanity labels — 'B1 by December' is a plannable goal; 'fluent someday' is not.

do: Read the CEFR self-assessment descriptors and write down which level you are targeting for listening, speaking, and reading separately.

children.title: Why-Clarity

learn.summary: Research on second-language motivation (notably Zoltan Dornyei's work on the 'ideal L2 self') shows that learners who can vividly picture themselves using the language persist far longer than those chasing abstract self-improvement. 'Talk to my grandmother in Cantonese' beats 'be smarter' every time. Your why also dictates your syllabus: a heritage speaker, a traveler, and an exam-taker should study very different things.

do: Write three specific scenes of future-you using the language (who, where, saying what). Keep the list in your study notebook.

children.title: The Time Budget

learn.summary: Consistency beats intensity: 30 minutes daily (about 180 hours a year) reliably outperforms a 3-hour Sunday binge, because spaced exposure is how memory consolidates. Treat 'dead time' — commutes, dishes, walks — as listening time, and reserve seated time for the hard work of speaking and study. Track hours, not streaks; hours are the input FSI's numbers are built on.

do: Audit one week: log every study minute in a note, then set a sustainable weekly hour target based on what actually happened.
